BENCHMARKSNOVEMBER 2026

quench.run / updated 17 November 2026

# Quench benchmarks

Every number Quench publishes, with its date, configuration and the tests where Quench loses.

With the JIT off in every engine, Quench scores 1.49x to 2.57x (14 Nov 2026) the faster of Node --jitless and Bun on all 8 V8-v7 benchmarks, at 0.28x to 0.55x their peak memory on 7 of 8. On the broader JetStream 3 suite it scores 34.3 against Node 39.7 and Bun 32.2, at 28.5 MB peak memory against 110.1 MB and 47.7 MB. The JIT tiers and AOT have no published compute speed numbers yet. AOT startup: a strict AOT hello world is a 4,896-byte executable that starts in 0.96 ms with 1.3 MB peak RSS (25 November 2026).

## V8-v7, JIT off (14 November 2026)

Interpreter only in every engine: quench --no-jit, node --jitless, and Bun with BUN_JSC_useJIT=0. Score is the suite's own score (higher is better). Memory is peak RSS (lower is better). "vs best" divides by the better of Node and Bun on that row.

Benchmark | Quench | Node --jitless | Bun JIT off | Score vs best | Quench RSS | Node RSS | Bun RSS | RSS vs best | 
richards | 2,759 | 1,220 | 1,529 | 1.80x | 6.4 MB | 43.5 MB | 15.9 MB | 0.40x | 
deltablue | 2,237 | 1,488 | 1,200 | 1.50x | 6.9 MB | 45.4 MB | 24.5 MB | 0.28x | 
crypto | 3,520 | 1,232 | 1,706 | 2.06x | 8.2 MB | 43.6 MB | 25.4 MB | 0.32x | 
raytrace | 8,084 | 3,780 | 2,711 | 2.14x | 7.1 MB | 50.1 MB | 25.8 MB | 0.28x | 
earley-boyer | 8,365 | 5,600 | 4,686 | 1.49x | 15.8 MB | 74.2 MB | 28.7 MB | 0.55x | 
regexp | 5,179 | 3,049 | 709 | 1.70x | 16.2 MB | 64.5 MB | 32.6 MB | 0.50x | 
splay | 6,940 | 3,722 | 2,995 | 1.86x | 58.7 MB | 326.0 MB | 54.9 MB | 1.07x | 
navier-stokes | 7,166 | 1,723 | 2,788 | 2.57x | 7.6 MB | 49.9 MB | 20.2 MB | 0.38x | 

Geometric means over the 8 rows: Quench 4,980 at 11.4 MB, Node 2,349 at 65.4 MB, Bun 1,979 at 26.8 MB. The geometric mean of Quench's per-row ratio to the better engine is 1.86x.

Weak spots: splay peaks at 58.7 MB, slightly above Bun's 54.9 MB (1.07x). earley-boyer is 1.49x, just under the project's 1.5x goal, and deltablue is exactly 1.50x.

## JetStream 3, JIT off (17 November 2026)

JetStream 3 has 75 tests in our harness. All three engines finish 56 of them, and only those 56 are compared, because a geometric mean over different test sets is not a comparison.

 | Quench | Node --jitless | Bun JIT off | 
Score, geomean (higher is better) | 34.3 | 39.7 | 32.2 | 
Peak RSS, geomean (lower is better) | 28.5 MB | 110.1 MB | 47.7 MB | 

On speed Quench is 0.86 times Node and 1.07 times Bun. On memory it uses 26% of Node's peak and 60% of Bun's, and has the lowest peak memory of the three on 51 of the 56 tests. Single-test noise is about 20%, so only the geometric means are meaningful.

### Best and worst rows (score vs the better of Node and Bun)

Best | Ratio | Worst | Ratio | 
gaussian-blur | 3.53x | babylonjs-scene | 0.44x | 
navier-stokes | 2.13x | babel-wtb | 0.39x | 
mandreel | 2.07x | chai-wtb | 0.39x | 
crypto | 1.89x | WSL | 0.38x | 
gbemu | 1.63x | async-fs | 0.36x | 
splay | 1.6x | validatorjs | 0.35x | 
earley-boyer | 1.6x | proxy-mobx | 0.25x | 
 | | octane-code-load | 0.23x | 

Quench wins on long-running hot loops: numeric kernels, emulators and the classic object-oriented benchmarks. It loses on tests dominated by loading and compiling code, by promises and async functions, and by proxies.

### Memory outliers outside the compared set

Test | Quench | Bun | Note | 
jsdom-d3-startup | 602 MB | 776 MB | Node did not finish it with the JIT off | 
babylonjs-startup-es6 | 562 MB | 339 MB | Node did not finish it with the JIT off | 
Kotlin-compose-wasm | 450 MB | did not finish | only Quench finished | 
babylonjs-scene-es6 | 226 MB | 189 MB | Node 210 MB | 

Details: Where Quench stands: JetStream 3 with the JIT off.

## Conformance

Suite | Result | 
Test262 (ECMAScript) | 53,353 passing, 0 failing, 53 waived; JIT off and on | 
WebAssembly spec suite | 67,124 of 67,124 | 

The 53 waived Test262 cases fail exactly the way Node fails them; each is listed with a reason in node-waivers.json and stays counted as a failure in every report.

## What is not measured yet

- Deno. Not in our harness yet, so no Deno numbers are published.

- JIT tiers. b-jit and u-jit are not yet competitive with V8 or JavaScriptCore with their JITs on; no comparison is published.

- AOT compute speed. No compute speed numbers are published for AOT-compiled programs; only startup, size and memory for strict images (hello world: 4,896 B, 0.96 ms, 1.3 MB; C 14 KB, 0.89 ms, 1.36 MB). The target is within 2x of Node and Bun.

## Method

One 4-core Linux machine, each test pinned to a core. Peak memory is the maximum resident set size of the process. The harness and raw results are in the repository; every number on this page can be rerun from it.

## About Quench

Quench is a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly runtime written in Rust. Test262: 53,353 passing, 0 failing. Interpreter, two JITs, and AOT to native executables. It is MIT licensed, early, and built from source with Cargo. Source: github.com/butaji/quench. Machine-readable summary: llms.txt.

RUST RUNTIMENOVEMBER 2026

quench.run / updated 20 November 2026

# A fast JavaScript runtime written in Rust

What Quench is, how fast it is today, and where it is still slower.

Quench is a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly runtime whose whole engine is written in Rust. With JIT turned off in every engine, it scores 1.49x to 2.57x (14 Nov 2026) the faster of Node --jitless and Bun on all 8 V8-v7 benchmarks, at a fraction of their memory. On JetStream 3 with JIT off it sits between them (34.3 vs Node 39.7 and Bun 32.2). Its JIT tiers are not yet competitive with Node or Bun with their JITs on.

## Quench vs Node.js, Bun and Deno

 | Quench | Node.js | Bun | Deno | 
Written in | Rust (engine and runtime) | C++ (V8) and JavaScript | Zig, C++ (JavaScriptCore) | Rust runtime, C++ engine (V8) | 
V8-v7 score, JIT off, geomean of 8 | 4,980 | 2,349 | 1,979 | not measured | 
V8-v7 peak memory, JIT off, geomean | 11.4 MB | 65.4 MB | 26.8 MB | not measured | 
JetStream 3 score, JIT off, 56 tests | 34.3 | 39.7 | 32.2 | not measured | 
JetStream 3 peak memory, JIT off | 28.5 MB | 110.1 MB | 47.7 MB | not measured | 
Test262 | 53,353 passing, 0 failing, 53 waived | not measured | not measured | not measured | 
JIT performance | JIT tiers not yet competitive | mature JIT | mature JIT | mature JIT (V8) | 
Packaged releases | no, build from source | yes | yes | yes | 

Benchmark rows: interpreter only in every engine (quench --no-jit, node --jitless, Bun with BUN_JSC_useJIT=0), one 4-core Linux machine. V8-v7 measured 14 November 2026, JetStream 3 on 17 November 2026. Bold marks the best measured value. Deno has not been measured; we do not publish numbers we have not run. Full tables and method.

## What is written in Rust

Everything that executes your program: the OXC-based front end, a register-bytecode interpreter with one 64-bit word per value, the object model and garbage collector, b-jit (copy-and-patch), u-jit (Cranelift) and the AOT compiler. Each tier is derived from one shared definition of each opcode, so the tiers agree on what a program means. Node-compatible node: APIs are also implemented in Rust.

## Where it is fast and where it is not

Quench is fastest on long-running hot loops: on JetStream 3 with JIT off, gaussian-blur runs at 3.53x the better of Node and Bun, navier-stokes at 2.13x, mandreel at 2.07x. It is slowest where code is loaded and compiled cold, on promise-heavy async code and on proxies: octane-code-load at 0.23x, proxy-mobx at 0.25x, async-fs at 0.36x. See benchmarks.

## Try it

git clone https://github.com/butaji/quench
cd quench
cargo build --release -p quench # interpreter + JIT tiers
cargo build --release -p quench --features aot # adds the AOT compiler
./target/release/quench app.ts

## Questions

### What is the fastest JavaScript runtime written in Rust?
Quench is a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly runtime whose engine is written in Rust. With JIT disabled in all engines, it scores 1.49x to 2.57x the faster of Node --jitless and Bun on all 8 V8-v7 benchmarks (14 November 2026). It has not been benchmarked against other Rust engines such as Boa, so we do not claim it is the fastest of them.

### Is Deno written in Rust?
Deno's runtime layer is written in Rust, but it executes JavaScript with V8, which is written in C++. Quench's engine itself (parser via OXC, interpreter, object model, garbage collector, JIT tiers and AOT compiler) is Rust.

### Is Quench faster than Node.js?
With JIT off: yes on all 8 V8-v7 benchmarks, and no on the JetStream 3 geometric mean (34.3 vs 39.7). With JIT on, Node is faster; Quench's JIT tiers are not yet competitive.

## About Quench

Quench is a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly runtime written in Rust. Test262: 53,353 passing, 0 failing. Interpreter, two JITs, and AOT to native executables. It is MIT licensed, early, and built from source with Cargo. Source: github.com/butaji/quench. Machine-readable summary: llms.txt.

# A Node.js alternative with low memory use

Peak memory measured against Node and Bun, including the tests where Quench uses more.

Quench is a JavaScript and TypeScript runtime with Node-compatible APIs, written in Rust. With JIT off, its geometric-mean peak memory on 56 JetStream 3 tests is 28.5 MB, against 110.1 MB for Node --jitless and 47.7 MB for Bun: 26% of Node's and 60% of Bun's. It has the lowest peak memory of the three on 51 of the 56 tests. It is early and has no packaged releases.

Benchmark | Quench | Node --jitless | Bun JIT off | 
richards | 6.4 MB | 43.5 MB | 15.9 MB | 
deltablue | 6.9 MB | 45.4 MB | 24.5 MB |

navier-stokes | 7.6 MB | 49.9 MB | 20.2 MB | 

## Where Quench uses more memory

On V8-v7 splay Quench peaks at 58.7 MB against Bun's 54.9 MB. On large startup workloads it can use much more: babylonjs-startup-es6 peaks at 562 MB against Bun's 339 MB, because programs from earlier iterations stay reachable and an idle function costs about 2.8 KB. Inside the 56 compared JetStream 3 tests, Quench is above the lowest engine on Sunspider, mandreel, the two doxbee tests and babylonjs-scene. Making function bodies lazy is the current fix.

## Why it is small

One 64-bit word per value, compact object layouts, a register-bytecode interpreter, and compiling a function body only on its first call.

## Try it

git clone https://github.com/butaji/quench
cd quench
cargo build --release -p quench # interpreter + JIT tiers
cargo build --release -p quench --features aot # adds the AOT compiler
./target/release/quench app.ts

## Questions

### What is a Node.js alternative with low memory use?
Quench is a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly runtime with Node-compatible APIs, written in Rust. With JIT off, its geometric-mean peak memory on JetStream 3 is 28.5 MB, against 110.1 MB for Node --jitless and 47.7 MB for Bun (17 November 2026).

### How much memory does Quench use for a small program?
On V8-v7 with JIT off, richards peaks at 6.4 MB, deltablue at 6.9 MB and raytrace at 7.1 MB, where Node --jitless needs 43.5 to 50.1 MB (14 November 2026).

### Can Quench replace Node.js today?
Not for production yet. Quench has no packaged releases and its Node API compatibility is still being built out, so expect gaps.

AOTNOVEMBER 2026

quench.run / updated 20 November 2026

# Compile JavaScript to a native executable

Quench's AOT compiler turns a JavaScript or TypeScript program into machine code, not a bundled script.

Quench compiles a JavaScript or TypeScript entry file and its imports ahead of time into one native executable: quench --build-aot app.ts -o app. The program is lowered to machine code with the same meaning as Quench's interpreter; the full interpreter and JITs are left out unless the program uses eval or new Function. AOT is experimental. With quench compile --strict-aot, a program that reads no run-time input compiles to an image with no engine at all: hello world is a 4,896-byte executable that starts in 0.96 ms with 1.3 MB peak memory, level with C (14 KB, 0.89 ms, 1.36 MB). Programs that read input fall back to a full image (readline REPL: 71.3 MB, 6.2 ms). Compute speed of AOT code is not published yet.

## Usage

cargo build --release -p quench --features aot
./target/release/quench --build-aot app.ts -o app
./app

## How it compares

 | Quench AOT | Node.js SEA | bun build --compile | deno compile | 
What goes into the binary | program compiled to machine code, plus runtime | script embedded in the node binary | bundle embedded in the Bun binary | program embedded in the Deno binary | 
Code runs as | precompiled native code | V8 interpreter and JIT at run time | JavaScriptCore at run time | V8 at run time | 
Full interpreter in the binary | only if eval or new Function is used | always | always | always | 
Published speed numbers | not measured | not measured | not measured | not measured | 
Maturity | experimental, build from source | stable | stable | stable | 

Quench has not benchmarked its AOT output against these tools, so this table describes mechanism only.

## One semantics

Each opcode's meaning is written once. The interpreter runs it directly, the JITs and the AOT compiler emit it as machine code. That is the interpreter specialized to what is known about the program (a Futamura projection), so an AOT-compiled program and an interpreted one agree. Background: AOT without a second compiler.

## Limits today

- Built and tested on Linux, from a source build with --features aot.

- Startup and size published only for programs with no run-time input; no compute speed numbers yet. The target is AOT code within 2x of Node and Bun.

- Node API compatibility is still being built out.

## The runtime around it

 | Quench | Node.js | Bun | Deno | 
Written in | Rust (engine and runtime) | C++ (V8) and JavaScript | Zig, C++ (JavaScriptCore) | Rust runtime, C++ engine (V8) | 
V8-v7 score, JIT off, geomean of 8 | 4,980 | 2,349 | 1,979 | not measured | 
V8-v7 peak memory, JIT off, geomean | 11.4 MB | 65.4 MB | 26.8 MB | not measured | 
JetStream 3 score, JIT off, 56 tests | 34.3 | 39.7 | 32.2 | not measured | 
JetStream 3 peak memory, JIT off | 28.5 MB | 110.1 MB | 47.7 MB | not measured | 
Test262 | 53,353 passing, 0 failing, 53 waived | not measured | not measured | not measured | 
JIT performance | JIT tiers not yet competitive | mature JIT | mature JIT | mature JIT (V8) | 
Packaged releases | no, build from source | yes | yes | yes | 

Benchmark rows: interpreter only in every engine (quench --no-jit, node --jitless, Bun with BUN_JSC_useJIT=0), one 4-core Linux machine. V8-v7 measured 14 November 2026, JetStream 3 on 17 November 2026. Bold marks the best measured value. Deno has not been measured; we do not publish numbers we have not run. Full tables and method.

## Questions

### How do I compile JavaScript or TypeScript to a native executable?
With Quench built with the aot feature, run quench --build-aot app.ts -o app, then ./app. The entry file and the modules it imports are compiled ahead of time into one native executable.

### Is the Quench AOT compiler faster than Node?
Compute speed of AOT code is not published yet. Startup is: with quench compile --strict-aot, a program that reads no run-time input compiles to a 4,896-byte hello world that starts in 0.96 ms, against 27.5 ms for Node running the script. Programs that read input still use a full image that starts in about 5 to 6 ms.

### Does an AOT-compiled Quench program include an interpreter?
The full interpreter and the JIT tiers are left out of the executable unless the program uses eval or new Function, which need to compile code at run time.

## About Quench

Quench is a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly runtime written in Rust. Test262: 53,353 passing, 0 failing. Interpreter, two JITs, and AOT to native executables. It is MIT licensed, early, and built from source with Cargo. Source: github.com/butaji/quench. Machine-readable summary: llms.txt.

# A Test262 compliant JavaScript engine

How Quench reports conformance, and what the 53 waivers are.

Quench passes 53,353 Test262 tests with 0 failing, with the JIT off and on. 53 cases are waived because they fail exactly the way Node.js fails them; they are listed with reasons and still counted as failures in every report. The WebAssembly spec suite passes 67,124 of 67,124.

## Results

Suite | Passing | Failing | Waived | Modes | 
Test262 | 53,353 | 0 | 53 | JIT off and JIT on | 
WebAssembly spec | 67,124 | 0 | 0 | | 

## How conformance is enforced

The Test262 runner in crates/quench-test262 reports every raw outcome. Test262 runs in interpreter and JIT modes before changes merge. A waiver must name a case that Node fails in the same way; it is rejected the moment the case starts passing or fails differently. The list: node-waivers.json. History: Test262 and the skip list.

## Quench vs Node.js, Bun and Deno

We run Test262 only on Quench. For other engines' Test262 results see test262.fyi.

## Questions

### Which JavaScript engine passes Test262?
Quench, a JavaScript runtime written in Rust, passes 53,353 Test262 tests with 0 failing and 53 waived, with the JIT off and on. The 53 waived cases fail exactly the way Node fails them and stay counted as failures in every report.

### What are the 53 waived Test262 tests?
Cases where Node.js itself fails in the same way, for example Node has no Error.prototype.stack accessor. Each is listed with a reason in node-waivers.json, and a waiver is rejected as soon as its case starts passing or fails differently.

### Does Quench pass the WebAssembly spec tests?
Yes: 67,124 of 67,124 WebAssembly spec suite cases.

AGENTSNOVEMBER 2026

quench.run / updated 20 November 2026

# A JavaScript engine for AI agent Code Mode

Running model-written code inside the harness: embedded, small, no JIT, full JavaScript and TypeScript.

Quench is a JavaScript and TypeScript engine written in Rust that embeds in an agent harness as a library and runs interpreter only, with no JIT. With the JIT off it scores 1.49x to 2.57x (14 Nov 2026) the best of Node --jitless and Bun on all 8 V8-v7 benchmarks, and five of them peak at 6.4 to 8.2 MB. Test262: 53,353 passing, 0 failing.

## What Code Mode needs

In Code Mode an agent writes a program and the harness runs it, instead of the model calling tools one at a time. A machine can host hundreds of such agents, each running code nobody reviewed. The engine has to live inside the harness, stay small per instance, run without a JIT, and run whatever the model wrote.

## The QuickJS slot, with more speed

Today the usual split is QuickJS for simple scripts and V8 for complex ones. Quench aims at QuickJS's place (small, embedded, interpreter only) with an interpreter well ahead of the ones in V8 and JavaScriptCore. Quench has not been benchmarked against QuickJS yet; that comparison is next and will be published either way.

V8-v7, JIT off | Quench RSS | Node --jitless RSS | Bun JIT off RSS | Quench score vs best | 
richards | 6.4 MB | 43.5 MB | 15.9 MB | 1.80x | 
deltablue | 6.9 MB | 45.4 MB | 24.5 MB | 1.50x | 
raytrace | 7.1 MB | 50.1 MB | 25.8 MB | 2.14x | 
navier-stokes | 7.6 MB | 49.9 MB | 20.2 MB | 2.57x | 
crypto | 8.2 MB | 43.6 MB | 25.4 MB | 2.06x | 

Peak RSS per process and score relative to the faster of Node and Bun, interpreter only in every engine (quench --no-jit, node --jitless, Bun with BUN_JSC_useJIT=0), one 4-core Linux machine, 14 November 2026. The other three benchmarks use more memory (earley-boyer 15.8 MB, regexp 16.2 MB, splay 58.7 MB against Bun's 54.9 MB). All rows and method.

## Embeddable and Rust-native

quench-runtime is a Rust library. The harness creates a Runtime with its own Host, exposes its tools to the generated code as host functions, and can stop runaway code from another thread with an execution interrupt. Generated code runs in the harness's own process, with no subprocess and no IPC. It is not on crates.io yet and the API will still change.

## No JIT required

--no-jit, which is also the library's default mode, runs the interpreter only, WebAssembly included. No machine code is generated while untrusted code runs. That takes JIT compiler bugs off the attack surface and leaves an attacker far less control over the machine code that executes, which Spectre-style attacks rely on. Every speed number on this page is with the JIT off. Quench is still not a sandbox on its own: isolation and resource limits come from your host.

## Full JavaScript and TypeScript

Test262 passes 53,353 tests with 0 failing (details). TypeScript runs directly with no build step, and Node-compatible node: APIs are available. Code a model writes just runs, with no "Lua needs a C extension for that" step, and models write JavaScript and TypeScript far better than Lua.

## Limits today

Quench is early: no packaged releases, Linux, built from source with Cargo. The embedding API is unstable. The per-instance memory of many runtimes in one process, and a comparison with QuickJS, are not published yet. On the broader JetStream 3 suite with the JIT off, Quench scores 34.3 against Node's 39.7 and Bun's 32.2, at 28.5 MB against 110.1 MB and 47.7 MB.

## Questions

### What is a good JavaScript engine for AI agent Code Mode?
Code Mode needs an engine that embeds in the harness, stays small per instance, can run without a JIT, and runs full JavaScript and TypeScript. Quench is built for that: a Rust library, interpreter only by default, Test262 53,353 passing and 0 failing. With the JIT off it scores 1.49x to 2.57x (14 Nov 2026) the best of Node --jitless and Bun on V8-v7.

### Is Quench faster than QuickJS?
Not measured yet. Quench aims at the slot QuickJS fills (small, embedded, interpreter only) with more speed, and its interpreter already beats the interpreters in V8 and JavaScriptCore on all 8 V8-v7 benchmarks. A QuickJS comparison is next and will be published either way.

### Why run agent code without a JIT?
A JIT writes new machine code at run time, shaped by the program it runs. Without one, JIT compiler bugs are off the attack surface and an attacker has far less control over the machine code that executes, which Spectre-style attacks rely on. The engine is still not a sandbox on its own: isolation and limits come from the host.

### How much memory does each Quench run use?
With the JIT off, five of the eight V8-v7 benchmarks peak at 6.4 to 8.2 MB of RSS per process, against 43 to 50 MB for Node --jitless and 16 to 26 MB for Bun. The per-instance cost of many runtimes embedded in one process has not been published yet.

## About Quench

Quench is a JavaScript, TypeScript and WebAssembly runtime written in Rust. Test262: 53,353 passing, 0 failing. Interpreter, two JITs, and AOT to native executables. It is MIT licensed, early, and built from source with Cargo. Source: github.com/butaji/quench. Machine-readable summary: llms.txt.

Related: benchmarks · JavaScript runtime in Rust · low-memory Node.js alternative · compile JavaScript to a native executable · Test262 conformance · JavaScript for AI agents

URL: https://quench.run/blog/hello-world-in-4896-bytes/

blog / 25 November 2026 · 5 min read · aot

# Hello world in 4,896 bytes: AOT as the JIT run at build time

Quench now compiles a JavaScript hello world to a 4,896-byte native executable that starts in 0.96 ms with 1.3 MB of memory, level with C. No second compiler: the build runs the program through the same specializer as the JIT and keeps only what is left.

Here is the smallest program we care about:

// hello.js
console.log("Hello world!")

And here is what Quench does with it on 25 November 2026:

$ quench compile --strict-aot hello.js -o hello
$ ls -l hello
-rwxr-xr-x 1 dev dev 4896 hello
$ ./hello
Hello world!

4,896 B
executable
C hello: 14 KB

0.96 ms
startup
C hello: 0.89 ms

1.3 MB
peak RSS
C hello: 1.36 MB

A day earlier the same program compiled to an 84.8 MB executable. This post is about what changed, and why it is not a hello-world trick.

## The numbers

console.log("Hello world!")| Executable| Startup| Peak RSS| 
Quench strict AOT image| 4,896 B| 0.96 ms| 1.3 MB| 
Quench AOT image, 24 November| 84.8 MB| 6.16 ms| 3.7 MB| 
C, gcc -O2, dynamic glibc, stripped| 14 KB| 0.89 ms| 1.36 MB| 
Node 22 running the script| (runtime)| 27.5 ms| 36 MB| 

One 4-vCPU x86 Linux machine, wall time and peak resident memory from a small C harness that spawns the process and waits for it. A later rebuild on 25 November measured 4,880 bytes, 0.99 ms and 1.2 MB, which is the run-to-run noise of this box. The build itself takes 0.15 s.

## Why it used to be 85 MB

Every Quench executable used to link the whole engine. Asking the linker why the parser stayed in a hello-world image gave a chain that explains everything: the image starts the generic VM, the VM can call a user function, a user function can hit code that was never compiled, and compiling it needs the parser. Once the VM is in, so are the interpreter, both JITs, WebAssembly, ICU, compression and TLS.

Trimming that graph edge by edge might reach a few megabytes. It can never reach C's size class, because the image still contains a JavaScript engine. To get there the image has to stop being "the engine plus your program".

## The first Futamura projection, at build time

Quench's design rule is that the interpreter is the only definition of what JavaScript means, and every other tier is that interpreter specialized to what it knows. We wrote about it in One interpreter, four outputs and AOT without a second compiler. The JIT specializes to facts it learns while the program runs. AOT is the same specializer run earlier, against facts known at build time.

With one source of truth for everything, AOT is just a particular case of JIT.

Specializing an interpreter to a program is the first Futamura projection: the result is a compiled program. Its coarsest form is also the simplest. The build runs the entry file against the same realm the image would start with, and keeps going until the program reads its first dynamic input: something a later run could see differently, such as its arguments, the environment, a file, the clock or standard input.

Everything computed before that point is the same in every run, so the image does not need the code that computed it. It only needs the program's effects: which bytes went to which descriptor, in what order, and the exit status.

Hello world reads no dynamic input at all. Its residual program is one write of 13 bytes to descriptor 1 and an exit status of 0. Quench emits that as a no_std Rust program that calls write and returns, and links it with the system C library. That is the whole 4,896-byte executable. There is no engine inside it because nothing is left for an engine to do.

## Why this is not a special case

Nothing in the compiler knows about console.log or about hello world. The rule is general: evaluate up to the first dynamic input, keep the effects. A program that builds a table, formats a report and prints it, reading nothing from outside, compiles the same way. The work it did at build time costs nothing at run time.

The rule is also strict in the other direction. If a program does read a dynamic input, the build stops there, says which input it was, and does not pretend. That half of the design is the subject of the companion post.

## What it does not do yet

Most real programs read an input in the first few lines. A command-line tool reads its arguments, a REPL reads standard input. For those, the strict image is refused today and the compile falls back to the full image, which still works and is still large. Our current target is a readline REPL, and the gap there is wide: we wrote down where it stands.

The next stage keeps more than effects. The build saves the heap at the program's first wait for input, and the code that runs after it (the input handlers) is compiled against that saved heap by the same JIT specializer, linking only the runtime services it still calls. The hello-world image is the end point of that pipeline for a program with no inputs. Every other program should land somewhere between 4.9 KB and the full engine, in proportion to how much of it really depends on run time.

---
URL: https://quench.run/blog/strict-aot-refuses-and-names-the-input/

blog / 25 November 2026 · 5 min read · aot

# Strict AOT: a compiler that refuses, and names the input

Running a program at build time is only safe if the build never bakes in something a later run would see differently. Quench's strict AOT mode is sound by construction: host operations off an allow-list are refused before they run, and the build names the input it could not fold.

Quench's strict AOT mode runs your program at build time and keeps only what it left behind. For a program that reads nothing from outside, that is a few kilobytes of output replay, as described in Hello world in 4,896 bytes.

Running code at build time has an obvious failure mode. If the build reads a file, the image contains the build machine's file. If it reads the clock, every run starts at the same instant. If it reads process.argv, every run gets the build's arguments. A compiler that does this produces a binary that is fast and wrong.

So strict AOT is built around one question: is this value the same in every future run? If the answer is not a proven yes, the build stops there.

## An allow-list, not a deny-list

Every way a Quench program touches the outside world goes through a named host operation. Strict AOT lets a short list of them run at build time, in aot/prefix.rs:

- Loading the program's own modules (require and the builtin module views). The sources are what the image is compiled from, so they are static by definition.
- Writes to stdout and stderr. They run against a recorder, not the terminal. The recording becomes the image's effects.
- Exit status: process.exitCode and process.exit(n).
- Asking for standard input. This only marks a read as wanted. The wait for it is where evaluation ends.

Everything else is a dynamic input: files, the terminal, timers, the network, child processes. A host operation that is not on the list is refused before it runs, and the refusal ends the run. It cannot be caught. We checked that with fs.writeFileSync inside a try: the build stops and no file is written.

A new host operation is dynamic until someone proves otherwise. Forgetting to classify one makes the build refuse, never makes it wrong.

A deny-list would fail the other way: the first operation nobody thought about would be baked silently into every binary.

## Inputs that hide in plain sight

Some inputs are not host calls at the point of use. They are values the runtime prepared at start-up. Quench handles those three ways:

- Process identity and environment (process.argv, execPath, pid, process.env) are lazy. They are not filled in until the program reads them, and reading them is a refused host operation.
- The clock, the local time zone and Math.random are noted by the runtime when used, so the build knows the result depended on them.
- Whether a stream is a terminal. This one surprised us. console.log of a non-string colours its output when stdout is a terminal, so even a constant program depends on where it runs. Our first build baked process.stdout.isTTY from the build worker's own descriptors. That was a soundness bug, and it is now an input like any other.

## Refusing with a name

A refusal is a diagnostic, not a crash. The compile report names the first dynamic input the run reached, then the compile falls back to the full image, which runs the program normally. These are four small programs on 25 November 2026:

Program| Strict outcome| Executable| 
console.log("hello")| image, no engine linked| 4,880 B| 
print process.argv| refused: the process identity (process.argv, execPath, pid)| full image| 
read a file named on the command line| refused: the process identity| full image| 
readline REPL| refused: standard input, after it waits for it| full image| 

The readline row is the interesting one. Its refusal is not "it reads stdin". The build evaluated everything up to the point where the program waits for a line: module loading, creating the interface, writing the prompt. Only then did it stop. That is exactly the prefix the next stage will keep as a saved heap instead of throwing away.

## Small inputs become variants

Refusing every input would make strict AOT useless for anything that prints a number. But some inputs have only a few possible values. Whether descriptor 1 is a terminal has two.

For those, the build does what partial evaluation calls "The Trick": it evaluates the program once per value the program actually distinguishes, and the image starts with a guard that picks the matching variant. Quench asks up to three yes-or-no questions per image (today: whether each of stdin, stdout and stderr is a terminal), and only the ones the program really read. The image calls isatty() at start and replays the right recording. A fourth question refuses the strict image and names it.

The same mechanism is meant to carry other small inputs later: whether an environment variable such as NO_COLOR is set, platform facts, how many arguments were passed.

## Why be this strict

Startup snapshots and build-time evaluation are not new. What we want from Quench is that the fast binary and the slow interpreter can never disagree. The interpreter is the only definition of JavaScript in the engine. The JIT and AOT are specializations of it, and a specialization is only correct if every fact it relied on holds in every run. For the JIT, a guard checks the fact at run time. For AOT, the fact has to be proved at build time, or the build has to say it could not.

That is the trade we picked: a strict build that sometimes says no, and names why, over a permissive one that is occasionally wrong.

---
URL: https://quench.run/blog/chasing-a-sub-megabyte-readline-binary/

blog / 25 November 2026 · 5 min read · aot

# Chasing a sub-megabyte readline binary

A small TypeScript compiler turns a readline REPL into a binary under 1 MB that starts in about 1 ms. Quench's is 71 MB and starts in 6.2 ms. Where the megabytes go, what we have cut so far, and the general plan to close the gap without a single readline-specific path.

This is a post about a benchmark we are losing.

The program is a 49-line TypeScript REPL built on node:readline: it prints a prompt, keeps history, completes command names, answers help, add, echo, upper and history, and exits on quit. It is the kind of program people want to ship as one small executable. scriptc, a compiler that translates a typed subset of TypeScript to native code, does that very well, and it is the bar we set ourselves for size and startup.

readline REPL, 25 November 2026| Executable| Startup to exit on quit| Peak RSS| 
scriptc build, same machine| 903 KB| 1.05 ms| 2.36 MB| 
Quench AOT, 24 November| 85.0 MB| 7.8 ms| 5.6 MB| 
Quench AOT, 25 November| 71.3 MB| 6.2 ms| 4.42 MB| 

One 4-vCPU x86 Linux machine, median wall time and peak RSS of the process from start to exit with quit on stdin. We are about 80 times larger, 6 times slower to start and twice the memory. The goal is about 1 MB and about 1 ms, reached only with optimizations that help every program.

## Where 85 MB went

The link map of the image, by origin:

What| Size| 
Engine and runtime code| 20 MB| 
SQLite engine| 10 MB| 
Node host code| 9 MB| 
Copy-and-patch JIT stencil tables| 6.6 MB| 
Cranelift JIT| 5.8 MB| 
ICU, zstd, brotli, Wasm, parser and more| about 6 MB| 
Unwind tables| 4.4 MB| 
OpenSSL| 3.4 MB| 

A REPL that never opens a database carried a SQL engine. The cause was one static table listing every host operation. Because the table referenced every module, the linker could not drop any of them. Turning off the JITs does not fix that: the no-JIT image was still 78 MB.

## What we have cut so far

Link only the host operations a program can reach. Each image now gets its own operation table, built from what the program can actually call, and heavy module state such as SQLite is created on first use. The image went from 85.0 MB to 71.3 MB, and the linker confirms no SQL code is left. Startup did not move. Unused code costs disk, not time.

Lay out start-up code together. Profiling start-up showed about 2,600 page faults per run at roughly 1.2 µs each. Ordering the functions that start-up runs next to each other took readline from 7.0 to 6.2 ms in back-to-back runs and 5.35 to 4.42 MB, and a smaller tool that prints its arguments from 5.6 to 4.9 ms.

Save the program at its first wait. The build now runs the REPL until it blocks on standard input, saves the runtime there (a 257 KB snapshot) and records the prompt it printed. A resumed run restores the snapshot and enters the event loop without running the entry again. Its output is identical to a full run for every command, and it exits on quit in 5.8 ms against 9.4 ms for the full run in the same harness. The engine is still linked, so memory does not drop yet.

## Why trimming is not the plan

Each of those cuts is real, and none of them gets to 1 MB. As long as the image contains a general JavaScript engine, it is the size of a general JavaScript engine. The way out is the same one that took hello world to 4,896 bytes: the image should contain only the code that is left after the build has used everything it knows.

For readline, what the build knows is a lot. At the first wait, the modules are loaded, the interface exists and the prompt is written. What remains is the line handler: split a line, look up a command, format a reply, write it. Three steps get there:

- Natives become staged rows. Much of Node's API in Quench is Rust code the specializer cannot see through. Each native the handler reaches (console writes, stream push, event emit, line splitting) is being rewritten as a staged row: a guard every tier runs, a small typed primitive the image can link on its own, and the general native as the fallback. The first row, the plain-string path of console.log, matches Node on all three tiers.
- Specialize the handlers at build time. The JIT specializer compiles the pending callbacks against the saved heap, so global lookups, method identities and constant strings fold.
- Link only what the residual calls. Runtime services become named symbols, the heap ships as read-only data mapped at a fixed address, and the linker keeps only what the handler code references.

The rule for this work: no optimization that only helps readline. Every change has to be one the interpreter, the JIT and AOT share.

## Why publish a losing number

Because the number is the point. Quench's AOT design bets that one specializer, run at build time, can produce binaries in the same class as compilers that only accept a subset of the language, while keeping all of JavaScript. Hello world says the bet can pay off at the small end. Readline is the first program where the program does something after start-up, and it is where the bet is tested. We will update this table as it moves, including if it stops moving.

URL: https://quench.run/blog/incremental-build-from-538-to-224-seconds/

blog / 25 November 2026 · 5 min read · build

# From 538 to 224 seconds: rebuilding a JavaScript engine faster

A one-line change in the arithmetic of Quench's interpreter took 538 seconds to rebuild. Two days of profiling LLVM, sharding generated code and refusing any change that cost a single instruction at run time brought it to 224 seconds. What worked and what we rejected.

Quench generates a lot of code. Each JavaScript operation is written once as a staged row, and the build expands those rows into the interpreter's handlers, thousands of copy-and-patch JIT stencils and the pieces the optimizing JIT and AOT reuse. That is how one definition feeds four outputs. It is also why touching the definition of + is expensive.

Our worst case is a one-line edit to arithmetic in staged/numeric.rs, rebuilt incrementally with the experiment profile on a 4-core machine. On 23 November 2026 it took 538 seconds. The project's rule is that an incremental build over five minutes is a bug, so this was a bug.

224 s
worst incremental build
was 538 s on 23 November

0
Ir cells worse
on the instruction-count gate

8 / 8
V8-v7 rows
pass on all three tiers

## The rule that made it hard

Making a build faster is easy if run-time speed can drop: inline less, split more, let LLVM see less. Quench does not allow that trade. Every change runs through an instruction-count gate on hundreds of small operations in three tiers, and the build work is held to the same rule as any other change: nothing may get slower. Several of the most effective build-time ideas below were rejected for that reason.

## Where the time went

The first profile settled one question: the build was CPU-bound. It spent about 1,850 CPU-seconds, so even perfect scheduling on 4 cores could not go below about 460 seconds. Tweaking job order was pointless. The code volume had to go down.

Most of that CPU was LLVM optimizing code it would soon throw away. Rows are built from #[inline(always)] pieces. A piece that dispatches over, say, 16 register placements gets copied into every row with all 16 arms, and only after inlining does LLVM discover that the row uses one of them. One family of 66 fused loop-test rows took about 7 seconds of LLVM each. In the stencils, the placement arms were 95% of a row's IR before optimization.

## What moved the number

Change| Worst incremental build| 
Starting point, 23 November| 538 s| 
Fused loop tests without a fixed comparison dispatch their record's own row instead of inlining every comparison| 481 s| 
Stencil placement helpers fold to the row's place before they inline| 424 s| 
Loop tests shared as one row per comparison; dead Wasm forms removed| 327 s| 
Stencil table stored as binary files; shared build cache read only on a fresh target| 293 s on its base, 320 s after upstream growth| 
Stencil frame reads: pick the place, then one 24-arm dispatch instead of 48| 295 s| 
Numeric rows in their own codegen modules; index and store rows re-weighted across shards| 224 s| 

The line is not monotonic, and that is honest: the engine kept growing while the build work went on, and upstream changes added about 140 CPU-seconds between two of the steps. Each step was measured against its own base.

The last step shows the shape of most of the wins. About 75 numeric rows had been spread by hash across all 16 generated-row modules and all 8 shards of each sharded handler family. An edit to arithmetic therefore recompiled every one of them. Giving numeric rows their own modules meant the same edit recompiles only those, and the engine's share fell from 597 to 338 CPU-seconds.

## What we rejected

The gate turned down more ideas than it accepted:

- Re-hashing every row into new modules. Faster to build, but 12 no-JIT cells got 17 to 84 instructions slower because closures moved out of line. Only numeric rows moved in the end, and everything else stayed in place.
- Always inlining runtime placement code in stencils. 27% less stencil CPU, but LLVM merged compare branches differently and one cell cost 25 more instructions.
- Passing the stencil hole as a run-time value. 18% faster to build, and a register allocation change cost another cell 6 instructions.
- Moving the Wasm GC call-out out of JavaScript rows. 302 KB less code, and 1 to 5 more instructions on 49 cells because LLVM spent the freed inline budget elsewhere.
- Re-landing a codegen unit split. 535 cells got worse. Moving generic instances into other units costs inlining in many places at once.

LLVM's inline budget is a shared resource. Freeing it in one place spends it in another, which is why every build-time change runs through the same run-time gate.

## What is next

224 seconds meets the five-minute rule with room to spare, and the remaining levers are already listed: the four out-of-line copies of the full Number step (about 74 CPU-seconds) and the arithmetic stencil shards (about 250). The broader lesson is about generated code in Rust. Compile time follows what LLVM sees before it optimizes, not what is left after, so the cheapest code to compile is the code that never gets inlined in the first place.

---
URL: https://quench.run/blog/where-quench-stands/

JETSTREAM 3NOVEMBER 2026

blog / 17 November 2026 · 4 min read · status

# Where Quench stands: JetStream 3 with the JIT off

Against Node and Bun with all JITs disabled, Quench sits between them on speed and well below both on memory. The full picture, including the tests where its memory is far too high.

This is a status report. It covers one configuration, measured on 17 November 2026: every JetStream 3 test, with the JIT turned off in Quench, in Node (--jitless) and in Bun (BUN_JSC_useJIT=0).

Why JIT off? Because that is where Quench is closest to its goals today, and because interpreter performance and memory are what matter for short-lived processes and constrained environments. The JIT tiers are covered in other posts, and they are not competitive yet.

## The headline

JetStream 3 has 75 tests in our harness. All three engines finish 56 of them. The comparison uses only those 56, because a geomean over different test sets per engine is not a comparison.

34.3
Quench score
Node 39.7 · Bun 32.2

28.5 MB
Quench peak memory
Node 110.1 · Bun 47.7

56
tests compared
of 75; all three engines finish them

Geometric means over 56 tests, JIT offQuenchNode --jitlessBun, JIT offscore (higher is better)34.339.732.2peak RSS, MB (lower is better)28.511047.7
One 4-core Linux machine, each test pinned to a core. Single-test noise is about 20%, so only the geomeans are meaningful.
On speed Quench is 0.86 times Node and 1.07 times Bun. On memory it uses 26% of Node's peak and 60% of Bun's.

The goal for this mode is 1.5 times the score of the better engine at half its memory. That means a score near 60 and memory near 24 MB. Memory is close. Speed needs about 1.7 times more.

## Test by test

Quench score relative to the better of Node and Bun (1.0 = equal), selected testsgaussian-blur3.53xnavier-stokes2.13xmandreel2.07xcrypto1.89xgbemu1.63xsplay1.6xearley-boyer1.6xbabylonjs-scene0.44xbabel-wtb0.39xchai-wtb0.39xWSL0.38xasync-fs0.36xvalidatorjs0.35xproxy-mobx0.25xoctane-code-load0.23x- parity
The seven best and the eight worst rows among the 56 compared tests.
The pattern is clear. Quench wins on tests that run a hot loop for a long time: numeric kernels, emulators, the classic object-oriented benchmarks. It loses on tests dominated by loading and compiling code, by promises and async functions, and by proxies.

## What the losses are made of

Cold code. octane-code-load evaluates a large script repeatedly. Each evaluation compiles about 380 functions. On a cold run of EarleyBoyer, 28% of all instructions were in the front end (parsing, analysis and bytecode generation) and one analysis pass ran three to five times per function.

The principle we are working to is that cold cost should be proportional to the code that runs, not the code that loads. The first step was making class methods lazy and compiling a function's body on its first call:

babylonjs-startup, cold run, instructions executedbefore lazy methods20.1 Gafter9.32 Gafter two follow-ups9.01 G
Billions of instructions, interpreter only. A 54% reduction from not compiling methods that are never called.
Async and boundary crossings. A callback from native code into JavaScript (a forEach callback, for example) cost 827 instructions where Node's interpreter spends 385.

Proxies and dynamic objects. proxy-mobx exercises exactly the paths a shape-based object model is worst at. A trapped read went from 777 to 186 nanoseconds in one change and it is still one of the two slowest rows.

## The memory outliers

The memory geomean covers the 56 tests every engine finishes. Outside that set there are tests where Quench's memory is plainly too high, and they should be shown.

Test | Quench | Bun | Note | 
jsdom-d3-startup | 602 MB | 776 MB | Node did not finish it with the JIT off | 
babylonjs-startup-es6 | 562 MB | 339 MB | Node did not finish it with the JIT off | 
Kotlin-compose-wasm | 450 MB | did not finish | only Quench finished | 
babylonjs-scene-es6 | 226 MB | 189 MB | Node 210 MB | 

On babylonjs-startup Quench's memory grows by about 54 MB per iteration: 97 MB after one iteration and 478 MB after eight. Part of it is retention: programs from earlier iterations stay reachable until the job ends. Part is how much an idle function costs. Quench holds about 2.8 KB per function across 18,655 functions, where V8 holds about 100 bytes for a function it has not needed yet. Laziness helps speed and memory at once here, which is why it is the current focus.

Inside the compared set, five tests have Quench above the lowest engine: Sunspider, mandreel, the two doxbee tests and babylonjs-scene.

## What is solid

- Conformance. test262 passes 53,353 tests with 53 waived and none failing, with the JIT off and on. The WebAssembly spec suite passes 67,124 of 67,124.
- Memory on ordinary programs. On 51 of the 56 compared tests Quench has the lowest peak memory of the three engines.
- Typical small-program footprint. Classic benchmarks such as Richards, DeltaBlue and Crypto peak at 12 to 14 MB, where Node needs 43 to 47 MB.

## What is next

In priority order for the interpreter:

- Pay for code only when it runs: lazy bodies everywhere, one analysis pass, smaller idle functions.
- Make a call a frame push and a return a pop, with one frame layout shared by every tier.
- Make crossing between native code and JavaScript cost no more than a JavaScript call.
- Bring every primitive operation inside its instruction budget.

And for the tiers above it: every tier faster than the one below on every test, and the optimizing tier within five times of C.

If any of this is the kind of problem you like, the repository is open and every number in this post can be reproduced from it.

FUTAMURAPROJECTIONS

blog / 12 November 2026 · 5 min read · architecture

# One interpreter, four outputs: Futamura projections in a JavaScript engine

Quench writes the meaning of each JavaScript operation once and derives the interpreter, a copy-and-patch JIT, an optimizing JIT and an AOT compiler from it. How that works, and an honest count of how far the code is from the design.

In 1971 Yoshihiko Futamura observed that if you have a program specializer and an interpreter, then specializing the interpreter to a particular source program gives you a compiled program. You never write a compiler. You write an interpreter and a specializer, and the compiler falls out.

It is one of the most elegant ideas in programming languages and it has mostly stayed in papers, with a few notable exceptions such as Truffle and, recently, weval for WebAssembly. Quench is built on it. This post explains how, and how much of it is real so far.

## The problem it solves

A JavaScript engine with an interpreter and two JIT tiers normally has three implementations of every operation. a + b is written once in the interpreter, once in the baseline compiler, and once in the optimizing compiler. They are supposed to agree. Engines have whole teams and fuzzers dedicated to finding where they do not.

Our own history shows the cost. In early November our JIT was slower than our interpreter on several benchmarks, and an audit found that that each improvement to the interpreter had to be made again, by hand, in each tier.

## One row per operation

In Quench the meaning of an operation is one generic function, called a row. It is written against an interface called a stage, which supplies the primitive steps: load a register, test a tag, add two integers, branch.

// Simplified. One definition of integer add with overflow check.
fn add<S: Stage>(s: &mut S, dst: Reg, a: Reg, b: Reg) {
 let x = s.read(a);
 let y = s.read(b);
 if s.both_int32(x, y) {
 let (sum, overflow) = s.add_overflow(x, y);
 s.branch_cold(overflow, |s| s.generic_add(dst, x, y));
 s.write_int32(dst, sum);
 } else {
 s.generic_add(dst, x, y);
 }
}

What that function does depends on which stage runs it.

One row, four stagesfn row<S: Stage>the only place the operation's meaning is writtenConcretecomputes the resultStenciloperands become holesEmitwrites compiler IREmit + relocIR, relocatableinterpreterknows nothingb-jitcopy-and-patchu-jitCranelift, optimizingAOTnative executable
Run on Concrete, the row is an interpreter handler. Run on the others, it generates code that does what the handler would have done.
- On the Concrete stage, s.read(a) reads a register and s.add_overflow adds. The row is the interpreter's handler.
- On the Stencil stage, at build time, operands are left as holes. The compiler produces a snippet of machine code per operation, and the b-jit later copies snippets end to end and patches the holes. That is copy-and-patch compilation, and compiling this way costs little more than a memcpy.
- On the Emit stage, s.add_overflow does not add anything. It appends an add instruction to Cranelift's intermediate representation. Run over a whole function, the rows write out an optimizing compiler's input.
- The same Emit stage with relocatable constants produces code that can be written to disk, which is AOT.

## Binding times: what each tier is allowed to know

The tiers differ only in how much they know when they generate code. We classify every operand by its binding time, the earliest moment its value is fixed.

Binding time | Example | Folded by | 
Static | register numbers, constants, jump targets | every native tier | 
Stable | an object's shape, a prototype, which function a name refers to | u-jit and AOT, under a registered dependency | 
Site | the type seen at one call site | u-jit, under one guard hoisted to where it is first proved | 
Dynamic | the actual number in a register | nothing; stays a run-time value | 

A Stable fact is the interesting one. It is not checked with a guard on every use. The compiled code registers a dependency, and if the fact ever changes (a prototype is modified, a function is reassigned) the code that relied on it is invalidated. Users of the fact pay nothing per use. The project's rule for this is "reactive, not guarded".

## Replacing thresholds with a price

When should a function move up a tier? Most engines use counters and constants. We had about thirty of them: warm up after 400 entries, re-optimize after 64 exits, inline up to 96 instructions.

The replacement is a single estimate of whether compiling pays for itself:

// simplified: the full rule also charges a per-entry cost
net(f, t) = remaining_work(f) × (1 − cost_ratio(t)) × interpreter_cost
 − compile_cost(f, t) × (1 + expected_deopts(f, t))

Remaining work is estimated from how often the function has run so far, on the assumption that code which has run n times will run about n more. For the irreversible decision to compile, a pessimistic bound of n/4 is used. Compile cost is a running fit of microseconds per instruction of IR. The tier with the highest positive net wins. Because the rule only chooses which tier runs and never changes the output, a wrong choice costs time and never correctness.

This is running as a shadow log beside the old thresholds, and on one benchmark it disagrees with them on 15 of 25 decisions. Working out which side is right is the current step.

## How far the code is from the design

Here is the honest count, from the repository's own census in mid-November.

46 / 268
opcodes
with their meaning in a shared row

~400
hand-written arms
of opcode logic still inside the tiers

601
fast-path handlers
37,800 lines, written by hand

An audit on 17 November put it more sharply: Futamura "holds on paper only". The meaning of an operation existed in four places: the general interpreter loop, 601 hand-written fast handlers, the shared rows, and a runtime operations module. The check that was supposed to stop tiers from re-implementing semantics counted opcode names, not logic, so logic could move under a different name and pass.

That audit is why the work now in progress has a simple target: one row per opcode, the interpreter's handler being that row on the Concrete stage, and a shrink-only count of every per-opcode decision that lives anywhere else. The list of hand-written arms can only get shorter.

## Why bother

Because the alternative does not converge. With three hand-written implementations, every optimization is three pieces of work and every bug fix is three chances to miss one. With one, an interpreter improvement is automatically a JIT improvement and an AOT improvement. The design does not make any single tier faster by itself. It makes the engine something a small team can keep correct while making it fast.

## Further reading

- Futamura, "Partial evaluation of computation process: an approach to a compiler-compiler" (1971)
- Würthinger et al., "Practical partial evaluation for high-performance dynamic language runtimes" (PLDI 2017)
- Xu and Kjolstad, "Copy-and-patch compilation" (OOPSLA 2021, arXiv 2011.13127)
- Xu and Kjolstad, "Deegen: a JIT-capable VM generator for dynamic languages" (arXiv 2411.11469)
- Fallin and Bernstein, "Partial evaluation, whole-program compilation" (weval, PLDI 2025, arXiv 2411.10559)

AHEAD OF TIMECOMPILATION

blog / 7 November 2026 · 4 min read · aot

# AOT without a second compiler

We built a closed-world JavaScript-to-native compiler, measured it, and threw it away. Quench's ahead-of-time mode is the interpreter specialized to what is known at build time, and this is why.

Ahead-of-time compilation for JavaScript is an old wish: hand the tool a program, get back one native executable that starts instantly and needs no runtime installed. Quench has a mode for it.

$ quench --build-aot app.ts -o app
$ ./app

This post is about the design behind that command, and the version of it we discarded on 7 November 2026.

## The prototype we threw away

The first AOT design was a separate closed-world compiler. It read the whole program, assumed nothing could change at run time, and translated JavaScript to native code through its own lowering, independent of the interpreter and the JIT.

It worked, and it ran Richards at a score of 5,846. That was slower than our own JIT on the same program.

The reason was not subtle. The prototype knew the whole program but not the things that make code fast: which numbers are integers, what shape each object has, which function a call reaches. Numbers stayed boxed. Without those facts, "compiled" just means the interpreter's work unrolled into a longer listing.

And it was a second implementation of JavaScript semantics. Every language feature would need to be written, tested and kept in sync twice.

## The reversal

So we reversed the design. There is no separate AOT compiler in Quench.

AOT is the interpreter specialized to build-time facts. The JIT is the same specializer applied to run-time facts.
One specializer, two sources of factsJITAOTJS / TS / Wasmsourcebytecodeone record per opspecializerinterpreter rowsJIT codein memorybuild-time factscallees, shapes, int fieldsrun-time factsobserved types, hot sitesnative executablerelocatable image
The same code generator (Cranelift, driven by the interpreter's own operation definitions) produces both outputs. Only where the facts come from differs.
The whole-program knowledge that the prototype had is still used. It just becomes an input to the specializer:

- Callee identity. If only one function in the program is ever stored under a property name, a call through that name can bind to it.
- Build-time shapes. Object layouts that are fixed by the program text are known before it runs.
- Unboxed integer fields. A field only ever assigned integers can be stored as one.

TypeScript types belong on that list too. Quench parses TypeScript natively and keeps the types instead of erasing them, and the design is for them to drive specialization: a declared type picks the specialized code up front, and is checked once where a value enters typed code, since a cast or an any can make a declaration wrong at run time. After that one check the type is relied on like any other proven fact. This is being built out now.

## What happens to eval

A closed-world compiler has to refuse eval and new Function. Quench does not refuse them. The rule is static: if the program can reach eval or Function, the interpreter is linked into the executable, and dynamic code runs through it. If it cannot, the interpreter is left out.

Guards work the same way. In the JIT, a failed guard deoptimizes back to the interpreter. In an AOT image, the cold side of a guard goes to a compiled generic path, so the program keeps running native code even when an assumption fails.

## Where it stands

Honestly: it works and it is not fast yet.

Wall time, 7 November 2026 (ms, lower is better)Quench AOTQuench JITNodeRichards1,234 ms537 ms103 msNavierStokes1,263 ms385 ms412 ms
Production AOT build against the JIT of the same day and Node. AOT was 2.3 to 3.3 times slower than our own JIT.
16 / 16
V8-v7 images
link and pass with the source deleted

50,808
test262
of 53,406 pass as AOT images

36 / 46
primitives
more than 5x the C equivalent

Correctness came first. Every one of the sixteen JavaScript and TypeScript benchmark programs builds to an executable that runs correctly with the source files deleted. Speed is behind: on 7 November, 36 of 46 primitive operations took more than five times the instructions of the equivalent C, and a few (spread and destructuring, string building) took hundreds of times more.

The goal is an executable where every function is compiled and the code is within five times of C. Because AOT is the same specializer as the JIT, it does not have its own performance work. Every improvement to how the interpreter's operations specialize shows up in both. That was the point of the reversal.

## Why this is the right shape

A second compiler is two sets of bugs and two sets of performance work, forever. One specializer with two fact sources means:

- Identical behavior by construction. There is one definition of what a + b means.
- AOT inherits every JIT improvement and the other way round.
- The fallback is always there. Anything the specializer cannot prove still runs, through the same generic operation the interpreter uses.

The next post in this series covers the mechanism that makes "one definition" possible.

TEST262CONFORMANCE

blog / 23 July 2026 · 3 min read · conformance

# 4,367 class tests in two days, and what a skip list hides

Driving one test262 directory from 44 passing tests to all 4,367 taught us more about denominators than about classes.

test262 is the official ECMAScript conformance suite: more than 50,000 files, each one a small program that must run, throw, or fail to parse in a precisely specified way. In July 2026 Quench was a tree-walking interpreter with one rule: no bytecode, no JIT, nothing clever until conformance is done.

We split the suite into stages, one per directory, and worked through them in order. Stage 16 is the class statement tests.

test262 stage 16 (class statements), passing tests- 0- 1,175- 2,350- 3,525- 4,70021 Jul22 Jul23 Jul23 Jul23 Jul23 Jultests passing, by commit- 4,367
Pass counts as written in commit messages, 21 to 23 July 2026. The third point is 798 of 844: for most of 22 July the runner only saw 844 of the tests.
Forty-four to 4,367 in two days looks like a hockey stick. It is partly real work and partly a lesson.

## What the real work was

Class tests are a stress test for everything around classes. Private names, static blocks, computed keys, accessors, super in every position, and generator and async methods. A few of the fixes from those two days:

- Deep recursion. The interpreter had been recursive in Rust, so deep JavaScript recursion overflowed the native stack. On 9 July it moved to an explicit work stack (a Vec of pending steps).
- Generators by replay. One commit is titled "Count nested yields in generator replay". The title suggests that at that point a generator resumed by re-running its body and skipping the yields it had already passed. It was slow and it was correct enough to pass, which was the goal that month.
- Thrown values out of band. A fix on 12 July snapshots the pending thrown value around ToPrimitive, because a stale exception from an earlier conversion was leaking into a later one.

## What the lesson was

Look at the middle of the chart. On 22 July the count goes 511 of 4,367, then 644 of 862, then 798 of 844. The numerator rose and the denominator fell. The runner was skipping whole groups of files, so "94.5%" that evening meant 94.5% of the tests we had chosen to look at.

It had happened at a larger scale two days earlier. On 20 July a commit announced that all 93 stages were at 100%. That commit changed one file: the skip list. On 22 July we added a tool that counted honestly across every directory, and its first report read:

23/122 stages done, 1870/48581 tests passing (3.8%)

Both statements were true. Every stage passed every test it ran, and the engine passed 3.8% of the suite.

100%
20 July
stages passing, with skips

3.8%
22 July
of all 48,581 tests

4,367
23 July
class tests, none skipped

## The rules that came out of it

Three habits date from that week and are still how Quench counts conformance:

- The denominator is the suite. A pass rate is reported against every file in the directory. Skipped is a failure with a name.
- Skips carry a reason and an owner. The skip list records why each entry is there, and the list may only shrink. The same shrink-only rule later spread to every debt list in the repository.
- A passing test never starts failing. A change that turns a green test red does not land, whatever else it fixes.

By 23 July stage 16 was at 4,367 of 4,367 with nothing skipped. The interpreter underneath was still slow, and still a tree walker. That was fine. The plan was to make it correct first, and August was about to make "first" a lot more interesting.
